_note: Lane A figure catalogue. Each figure is a FIRST-CLASS OBJECT with its own figure_id, title, caption and labels, so the same figure can be recalled and shown in more than one place: beside a reference entry, beside a question, or on its own. `used_by` lists those places; it is a list, not a single owner. `covers` records which of a linked entry's authored items[] labels this figure renders, and verify.py checks it per entry. `layout` is chosen by the container at render time: compact (272-460px side pane), full (~680px question pane), expanded (enlarge control, notes sheet single column).

chem-mb-energy.title: Maxwell–Boltzmann energy distribution
chem-mb-energy.subtitle: Raising the temperature increases the fraction of particles beyond Ea
chem-mb-energy.alt: Two distribution curves of relative number of particles against particle energy. The higher-temperature curve is lower at its peak, broader and shifted right, so a larger shaded area lies beyond the vertical activation-energy marker. Illustrative data.
chem-mb-energy.note: Area beyond Ea estimates the fraction of collisions with sufficient energy.
chem-mb-energy.caption: Raising the temperature increases the fraction of particles beyond Ea

chem-mb-catalysis.title: Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution: effect of a catalyst
chem-mb-catalysis.subtitle: A catalyst lowers Ea, so more particles clear the barrier at the same temperature
chem-mb-catalysis.alt: One distribution curve of number of particles against kinetic energy at a fixed temperature, with two vertical activation-energy markers. The catalysed barrier sits to the left of the uncatalysed one, so the shaded area beyond it is larger. Illustrative data.
chem-mb-catalysis.note: Same temperature, same curve: only the barrier moves.
chem-mb-catalysis.unpublished: No published app.unit_reference_entries row with this title in Production (read 2026-10-10). It exists only as a seed candidate. The nearest published rows are the Unit 5 convention 'How a catalyst increases rate' and the Unit 3 vocabulary 'Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution'. Kept as a figure, excluded from coverage, and not production-eligible until an entry exists for it.
chem-mb-catalysis.caption: A catalyst lowers Ea, so more particles clear the barrier at the same temperature

chem-energy-profile-single.title: Single-step reaction energy profile
chem-energy-profile-single.subtitle: Reactants, one transition state, products
chem-energy-profile-single.alt: Energy plotted along the reaction coordinate. The curve rises from the reactant level to a single transition-state maximum, then falls to a product level below the reactants, so the reaction is exothermic. Illustrative data.
chem-energy-profile-single.caption: Reactants, one transition state, products

chem-energy-profile-multistep.title: Multistep reaction energy profile
chem-energy-profile-multistep.subtitle: Each elementary step contributes its own barrier; the largest sets the rate
chem-energy-profile-multistep.alt: Energy along the reaction coordinate for a two-step mechanism. The curve rises to a first transition state, falls to an intermediate, rises to a lower second transition state, then falls to products below the reactant level, so the overall reaction is exothermic. The first barrier is the larger of the two and sets the rate. Illustrative data.
chem-energy-profile-multistep.caption: Each elementary step contributes its own barrier; the largest sets the rate

chem-energy-diagram-process.title: Energy diagram for a process
chem-energy-diagram-process.subtitle: Products below reactants means energy is released: the process is exothermic
chem-energy-diagram-process.alt: Two energy levels joined by a falling curve. The final state sits below the initial state, so energy is released and the process is exothermic. Illustrative data.

chem-mass-spectrum.entry_title: Mass spectrum of a single element
chem-mass-spectrum.title: Mass spectrum of a single element
chem-mass-spectrum.subtitle: Magnesium: one peak per isotope, height set by natural abundance
chem-mass-spectrum.alt: Three vertical peaks at masses 24, 25 and 26. The peak at mass 24 is by far the tallest at about 79 percent, with smaller peaks near 10 and 11 percent. Peak position identifies the isotope and peak height gives its natural abundance.
chem-mass-spectrum.note: Isotopes differ in neutron count, not proton or electron count.
chem-mass-spectrum.values_note: Magnesium isotope masses and abundances are taken from the PUBLISHED AP Chemistry 1.2 explainer ('Mass Spectra of Elements'), which works the same figures and cites CED 1.2.A.1-2. verify.py independently recomputes the weighted average from them and requires 24.305, so the figure is self-consistent with its source. Kept as measured data, not illustrative.

used_by.title: Mass spectrum of a single element

chem-mass-spectrum.caption: Magnesium: one peak per isotope, height set by natural abundance

chem-pes.title: Photoelectron spectrum
chem-pes.subtitle: Nitrogen (1s2 2s2 2p3): one peak per subshell, height set by electron count
chem-pes.x_label: binding energy (MJ/mol), decreasing to the right
chem-pes.alt: Three peaks on a logarithmic binding-energy axis that decreases to the right, for nitrogen (1s2 2s2 2p3). The 1s peak sits far left at about 39.6 megajoules per mole with height two, then 2s at about 2.45 with height two, then 2p at about 1.45 with height three. Peak height is proportional to the number of electrons in that subshell, and the three heights sum to nitrogen's seven electrons. Illustrative values.
chem-pes.note: Electrons closer to the nucleus need more energy to remove.
chem-pes.values_note: Heights (2:2:3) and the binding-energy ordering are exact for nitrogen. The 1s value cross-checks against ~400 eV (~39.5 MJ/mol), but the 2s and 2p figures are standard AP teaching values that I could not trace to a primary table, so the figure is disclosed as illustrative rather than measured.
chem-pes.caption: Nitrogen (1s2 2s2 2p3): one peak per subshell, height set by electron count

chem-pe-internuclear.entry_title: Potential energy vs. internuclear distance graph
chem-pe-internuclear.title: Potential energy vs. internuclear distance
chem-pe-internuclear.subtitle: The minimum gives the bond length; the well depth gives the bond energy
chem-pe-internuclear.alt: Potential energy against the distance between two nuclei, for a single and a double bond. Each curve rises steeply at short distance, passes through a minimum, and approaches zero at large separation. The double-bond curve has its minimum at a shorter distance and a deeper well than the single bond. Illustrative data.
chem-pe-internuclear.note: Higher bond order: shorter bond, deeper well.

used_by.title: Potential energy vs. internuclear distance graph

chem-pe-internuclear.caption: The minimum gives the bond length; the well depth gives the bond energy

chem-approach-equilibrium.entry_title: Graphs showing the approach to equilibrium
chem-approach-equilibrium.title: Approach to equilibrium
chem-approach-equilibrium.subtitle: Concentrations change, then level off (figure 1 of 2)
chem-approach-equilibrium.alt: Concentration against time for a reactant and a product. The reactant curve falls and the product curve rises, and both flatten to constant values after which there is no net change. Illustrative data.
chem-approach-equilibrium.note: Flat lines mean no net change, not that the reaction has stopped.

labels: Concentration or partial pressure vs. time

chem-titration.entry_title: Titration curve (pH vs. volume of titrant)
chem-titration.title: Titration curve
chem-titration.subtitle: Weak acid with strong base: pH = pKa at the half-equivalence point
chem-titration.alt: pH against volume of titrant for a weak acid titrated with a strong base. The curve rises slowly through a buffer region, passes through pH equal to the pKa at half the equivalence volume, then rises steeply to an equivalence point above pH 7. Illustrative data.
chem-titration.note: pKa is read at the half-equivalence point, not the equivalence point.

used_by.title: Titration curve (pH vs. volume of titrant)

chem-titration.caption: Weak acid with strong base: pH = pKa at the half-equivalence point

chem-approach-equilibrium-rate.entry_title: Graphs showing the approach to equilibrium
chem-approach-equilibrium-rate.title: Approach to equilibrium: rates
chem-approach-equilibrium-rate.subtitle: Forward and reverse rates converge and become equal (figure 2 of 2)
chem-approach-equilibrium-rate.alt: Forward and reverse reaction rates against time. The forward rate falls and the reverse rate rises until the two meet at a common value and stay there. Equal rates, not zero rates, is what equilibrium means. Illustrative data.
chem-approach-equilibrium-rate.note: Equal rates, not zero rates: both processes continue.

used_by.title: Graphs showing the approach to equilibrium

chem-approach-equilibrium-rate.caption: Forward and reverse rates converge and become equal (figure 2 of 2)
